blocks.html: Every photo on your phone is made of millions of tiny coloured squares called pixels (picture elements). Zoom into a photo far enough and you can see them.

rows: Smallest dot of colour in an image
Pixels (or printed dots) per inch — decides print sharpness
300 DPI for good photo prints; screens need far less
Bits used per pixel to store colour
Space the file takes on disk
A phone photo is usually a few MB

blocks.html: Worked example: A photo of 4000 × 3000 pixels printed at 300 DPI will be 4000 ÷ 300 ≈ 13.3 inches wide and 3000 ÷ 300 = 10 inches tall.

rows: Made of shapes described by mathematics (lines, curves)
Best for logos, icons, diagrams, maps
Formats: JPEG, PNG, GIF, BMP, TIFF, WebP
Formats: SVG, EPS, AI, PDF (vector content)
Edited in Photos, Paint, GIMP, Photoshop
Old Windows bitmaps; very large files

items.html: Lossless compression makes the file smaller without throwing away any information; the original can be rebuilt exactly (PNG, GIF, ZIP files).
Lossy compression removes detail that the eye hardly notices to make the file much smaller; repeated saving reduces quality further (JPEG).

blocks.html: Did you know? Many online application forms (board registration, scholarship and job portals) ask you to upload a photo below a size limit — for example 50 KB — and a signature in JPEG. Knowing how to resize and compress a picture is a genuinely useful skill.
Older versions of Microsoft Office (2003 to 2010) included Microsoft Office Picture Manager for simple editing. It is no longer supplied, but the same tasks can be done with free tools:

rows: Crop, rotate, adjust light and colour, filters, red-eye, background blur
Resize, crop, text, shapes, quick annotations

blocks.caption: Figure 5.1 · Crop, resize and compress compared

rows: Cuts away unwanted edges; can set an aspect ratio such as 1:1 or 3:4
Turns the picture by 90° or mirrors it
Fixes a tilted horizon by a few degrees
Changes pixel dimensions; keep maintain aspect ratio ticked so the picture is not stretched
Paint → Resize (Ctrl + W); Photos → … → Resize image
Difference between light and dark areas
Strength of colours; zero saturation gives black and white
Fixes red eyes caused by camera flash
Separates the subject from the background
Reduces file size; choose JPEG quality
Paint → Save as → JPEG; Photos → Resize → choose a smaller size

blocks.html: If a photo is 4000 × 3000 and you need a width of 800, the height must be 800 × 3000 ÷ 4000 = 600 to keep the 4:3 ratio. Typing a different height would stretch or squash faces.

items.html: Cropping removes part of the picture (fewer pixels, smaller area shown).
Resizing keeps the whole picture but uses fewer (or more) pixels.
Compressing keeps the same pixel dimensions but stores them more efficiently, with some loss of detail in JPEG.

blocks.html: In Word, Excel and PowerPoint, the Picture Format tab offers: Crop (including Crop to Shape and aspect ratios), Corrections (sharpen, brightness), Colour, Artistic Effects, Transparency, Remove Background, Picture Styles and borders, and Compress Pictures (to reduce the size of the whole document before emailing).

items.html: Keep the original. Always edit a copy (Save As with a new name).
Respect copyright. Pictures found online belong to their creators. Use your own photos, images with a free licence (e.g. Creative Commons) or ones you have permission to use, and give credit.
Ask permission before posting someone's photo, especially of children.
Do not deceive. Editing a picture to spread false information, fake documents or to make fun of someone is unethical and can be a crime under cyber law (Chapter 6).
Check metadata. Photos may store location (GPS) information; remove it before sharing publicly.

Digital images are made of pixels; resolution, PPI/DPI, aspect ratio and colour depth describe them.
Raster images are made of pixels and suit photos; vector images are made of shapes and stay sharp when enlarged.
JPEG is lossy and suits photos; PNG is lossless with transparency; GIF supports simple animation; SVG is a vector format.
Picture Manager is no longer supplied; Photos, Paint, GIMP and mobile apps do the same jobs.
Common edits: crop, rotate, straighten, resize, brightness/contrast, saturation, red- eye, filters, text, background removal and compression.
Keep originals, respect copyright, ask permission and never edit pictures to deceive.
